prompt: How does resistance to a number usually arrive, by the lesson?

choices.text: As an open refusal to accept the finding in front of the whole meeting
choices.why: Rarely; it is usually more polite than that.

choices.text: As a formal complaint to the analyst's manager after the presentation
choices.why: Possible, and not the usual form.

choices.text: As a question about the analysis
choices.why: Definitions, months, method: each reasonable, together a wall.

choices.text: As silence
choices.why: Not the form described.

prompt: Which reasons for resisting a number does the lesson list? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Loss of standing
choices.why: Praised for 94.5% for years.

choices.text: Fear of blame
choices.why: The easiest defence is to doubt the number.

choices.text: Change fatigue
choices.why: The fourth initiative meets a shrug.

choices.text: Not understanding percentages
choices.why: Resistance is rarely about the arithmetic.

prompt: The warehouse staff warned that new streets are missing from the postcode lookup. What was that?

choices.text: Knowledge the analyst lacked, which made the pilot safer
choices.why: It is why the check is skipped only for addresses the lookup confirms.

choices.text: Obstruction
choices.why: It improved the plan.

choices.text: A reason to cancel
choices.why: It changed the scope, not the decision.

choices.text: Change fatigue
choices.why: It was a specific, useful warning.

prompt: Why is a new measure harder to accept than a new finding, by the lesson?

choices.text: Because measures are always computed by people from outside the team
choices.why: Faro's ended up computed by Diego, inside the team.

choices.text: Because a new measure needs a new dashboard tool to display it properly
choices.why: Tooling is not the issue.

choices.text: Because findings are usually ignored anyway, while measures are enforced
choices.why: Not the argument.

choices.text: It is permanent: amber every week
choices.why: A team that was green turns amber without doing anything differently.

prompt: Why did Faro's dashboard show both the overall and the first-delivery rate for a while?
hint: The old measure was not wrong.

choices.text: To avoid choosing which one is correct
choices.why: Both are correct.

choices.text: It was incomplete, not wrong, and showing both says so
choices.why: The team sees its old achievement still counted.

choices.text: Because the dashboard had space
choices.why: Not the reason.

choices.text: Ligeiro asked for it
choices.why: No.

prompt: Why did it matter that Diego rebuilt the first-delivery rate from his own data?

choices.text: Because Marina's version had a calculation error in the way it handled dates
choices.why: Nothing says it did.

choices.text: Because analysts in logistics are paid more and so their numbers count for more
choices.why: No.

choices.text: Your own analyst's number is one you defend
choices.why: Ownership turns the measure from an attack into the team's own.

choices.text: It was faster
choices.why: Not the reason.

prompt: A target somebody chose is a goal; a target imposed from outside is a ___.
Put the five ADKAR stages in order.
A team knows exactly what to do and does not want to. What does ADKAR say will not help?
hint: Which stage are they stuck at?

choices.text: More training, since knowledge is not where they are stuck
choices.why: They are stuck at desire.

choices.text: Talking about why
choices.why: That addresses desire, which may help.

choices.text: A role in the change
choices.why: That builds desire.

choices.text: A short-term win
choices.why: That can build desire.

prompt: Which two of Kotter's steps does the lesson say carry over to small changes?

choices.text: Create urgency and anchor the changes in the culture of the company
choices.why: Those are for organisation-wide change.

choices.text: Form a vision and communicate it to everybody in the organisation
choices.why: Heavy for one warehouse procedure.

choices.text: Remove obstacles and consolidate gains to produce even more change
choices.why: Not the two named.

choices.text: A coalition, and short-term wins
choices.why: Sandra, Diego and Paulo; and the first pilot weeks.

prompt: How does the lesson say to treat these models?

choices.text: As proven recipes that guarantee the change succeeds
choices.why: They are distilled from experience and have critics.

choices.text: As checklists that help you notice what you forgot
choices.why: Useful, and not experimental laws.

choices.text: As management fashion to ignore
choices.why: Your colleagues use them.

choices.text: As legal requirements
choices.why: No.

prompt: Why did Sandra, not Marina, put the first pilot week on the noticeboard?

choices.text: Because Marina was on holiday that week and could not do it herself
choices.why: Not in the story.

choices.text: Because analysts are not allowed to post notices in the warehouse
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: The win belonged to the team that made it
choices.why: Nobody had to be told how they were doing by an outsider.

choices.text: Sandra designed the pilot
choices.why: Her team ran it; the design was shared.

prompt: To one decimal place, what was the interior's late share in the first week of the pilot?
What is a pilot, besides a test of a cause, by the lesson?

choices.text: A way to postpone a decision that the manager does not want to make yet
choices.why: It had a date and a decision rule.

choices.text: A way to spend the remaining budget before the end of the quarter
choices.why: It cost no new money.

choices.text: A way to prove the analyst right in front of the whole company
choices.why: It belongs to the team, not the analyst.

choices.text: A way to let people find out
choices.why: A team that watches its own number fall does not need convincing.

prompt: The decision has been made. What does the lesson say about consulting people now?

choices.text: Say it is decided, and involve them in how, which is where their knowledge lies
choices.why: A fake consultation produces more resistance than none.

choices.text: Run a consultation anyway
choices.why: People notice it is for show.

choices.text: Skip them entirely
choices.why: Then they are not involved in how either.

choices.text: Reopen the decision
choices.why: Not the advice.

prompt: From which week of the pilot did the interior stay at or under 8%?
Why did Paulo's decision on 27 October take ten minutes?

choices.text: Because the results were so good that nobody wanted to discuss anything else
choices.why: Good results still need agreed criteria to be judged.

choices.text: The criterion, guardrail and rule were set in advance
choices.why: Nobody had to argue about what success meant.

choices.text: He had already decided
choices.why: He decided against the agreed rule.

choices.text: The meeting was short
choices.why: Length was not the reason.

prompt: What keeps the change in place after the roll-out? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The measure stays on the dashboard with its target
choices.why: Visible every week.

choices.text: It enters the logistics team's objectives
choices.why: Somebody is accountable.

choices.text: Checks at thirty, sixty and ninety days
choices.why: The ninety-day one reads the lagging measure.

choices.text: A celebration and no further measurement
choices.why: Without measurement, drift goes unnoticed.

prompt: Why is the ninety-day check the one that matters most?

choices.text: Because ninety days is the length of a quarter and the board meets quarterly
choices.why: Coincidence, not the reason.

choices.text: Because by ninety days the warehouse staff will have forgotten the old process
choices.why: Not the reason given.

choices.text: It is the first read of the lagging measure
choices.why: Cancellations of customers whose first box came after the change.

choices.text: Legal reasons
choices.why: No.

prompt: In early 2026, the autumn cohorts' cancellations have not fallen. What does the lesson say that result is?

choices.text: A failure to hide, since it contradicts the whole analysis and the pilot
choices.why: Hiding it is the worst option.

choices.text: Proof that the pilot data was wrong and the warehouse staff misreported it
choices.why: Jumping to blame repeats lesson 10's mistake.

choices.text: A reason to undo the change in the warehouse straight away
choices.why: Deliveries improved; the next analysis should find out why cancellations did not.

choices.text: Where the next analysis starts
choices.why: Saying in advance what would change your mind makes it useful, not embarrassing.
